passages.t: Magi from the east, and a troubled king
passages.happening:
Some time after Jesus is born in Bethlehem, visitors arrive in Jerusalem from the east. Matthew calls them Magi. They ask a dangerous question: “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews?” They have seen his star, and they have come to worship him (verse 2).

King Herod is shaken, and the whole city with him. He gathers the chief priests and the scribes, the experts in the Scriptures, and asks where the Messiah is to be born. They answer at once: in Bethlehem, as the prophet wrote. Herod then meets the Magi in secret, finds out exactly when the star appeared, and sends them to Bethlehem. Tell me when you find him, he says, so that I can worship him too. He is lying.
passages.hearers:
The Magi were not kings. The word meant a class of priestly wise men from Persia and the lands near it. The Greek historian Herodotus described them as a tribe of the Medes who read dreams and the heavens (Histories 1.101). By this time the word could mean a respected sage or, less kindly, a sorcerer. Matthew does not say how many came. The idea of three comes later, from the three gifts.

To ask Herod where the new King of the Jews is born was close to treason. Herod held that very title. Rome had made him king of Judea, and he ruled from 37 BC. But his family came from Idumea, south of Judea, and many Jews never fully accepted him. He was also famous for suspicion. The Jewish historian Josephus tells how he killed his own wife Mariamne and three of his sons when he feared they threatened his throne. Hearers who knew that would feel the danger in verse 3.

People in the ancient world widely believed that the heavens marked the birth and death of great rulers. Jewish readers also had an old prophecy about a star: Balaam saw that “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel” (Numbers 24:17).

Notice the irony. The scribes know exactly where the Messiah will be born. Bethlehem is only a short walk away. Yet the foreigners travel to find him, and the experts stay home.
passages.ot: The scribes quote Micah 5:2, about a ruler from Bethlehem, the small town where David was born. Matthew's wording differs from Micah's. Micah says Bethlehem is “small among the clans of Judah”; Matthew says it is “by no means least” (2:6), because now that the ruler has been born there, it is small no longer. The last line, “who will be the shepherd of My people Israel”, is borrowed from God's words to David in 2 Samuel 5:2. Matthew weaves the two together: the promised ruler is a king like David, and a shepherd.
passages.hard: What was the star? No one knows, and several answers have been proposed. In 7 BC the planets Jupiter and Saturn met three times in the night sky, which Johannes Kepler pointed to in the 1600s. Chinese records tell of a new object, perhaps a comet, seen for about seventy days in 5 BC. Others point to the moon passing in front of Jupiter in 6 BC, or to Jupiter and Venus close together in 2 BC. Some read Matthew's star as a sign from God that no natural event explains, since it goes ahead of the Magi and stops over a house (verse 9). Each of these is a proposal, not a proof. Matthew's point does not depend on settling it: God drew outsiders to his King, and Israel's own leaders did not come.
passages.asks: Herod heard about Jesus and saw a threat. The scribes knew all about him and did not move. The Magi knew least and travelled farthest. Which of the three is most like you? Knowing the right answers about Jesus is not the same as coming to him.

passages.happening:
The Magi set out, and the star goes ahead of them until it stops over the place where the child is. They are overjoyed. They come into the house, see the child with his mother Mary, and fall down and worship him. Then they open their treasures and give him gold, frankincense and myrrh.

Warned in a dream not to go back to Herod, they go home another way.
passages.hearers:
Notice that Matthew says ‘house’, not stable. By now the family seems to be living in Bethlehem, and the child may be a year old or more, since Herod later kills boys up to two years old (verse 16). The Christmas scene that puts shepherds and Magi side by side joins Luke's story and Matthew's.

The gifts were costly. Gold was the gift for a king. Frankincense and myrrh are sweet-smelling resins, gum from trees that grew in southern Arabia and the Horn of Africa, and they came north by caravan at great price. Frankincense was burned as incense in worship. Myrrh was used in perfume and medicine and for preparing bodies for burial. Around 180, Irenaeus read the three this way: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for one who would die and be buried (Against Heresies 3.9.2). Matthew does not say so himself, but it is an old and lovely reading.

‘Fell down and worshiped Him’ means the Magi bowed to the ground. That was how you honoured a king. Matthew's readers would also see more: in this Gospel, people worship Jesus again and again (14:33; 28:9, 17).
passages.ot: Hearers who knew their Scriptures would remember Isaiah 60, where nations come to Israel's light and “all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense” (Isaiah 60:6). And Psalm 72, a prayer for the king: “May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him” (Psalm 72:11). Those passages later shaped the idea that the Magi were kings. Matthew simply shows the hope beginning to come true. The nations have started to arrive.
passages.asks: The Magi gave Jesus the best they had and then went home changed, by another way. Worship in Matthew is not only feeling something; it is bowing down and giving. What would it mean for you to open your treasures to Jesus? And what road home might be different after you have met him?

passages.happening:
After the Magi leave, an angel again speaks to Joseph in a dream. Get up, the angel says. Take the child and his mother and run to Egypt, because Herod is going to search for the child to kill him. Joseph gets up that same night and goes. The family stays in Egypt until Herod dies.

Matthew adds a line from the prophet: “Out of Egypt I called My Son” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Egypt was a natural place to flee. It lay outside Herod's power, under direct Roman rule, and it had one of the largest Jewish communities in the world, above all in the great city of Alexandria. A Jewish family could find people who spoke their language and kept their faith.

Matthew's hearers would also feel how strange it was. Egypt was the land of slavery in Israel's story, the place God brought his people out of. Now Israel's Messiah has to run to Egypt to be safe from Israel's own king. The world has turned upside down.

Notice too how quickly Joseph obeys. He gets up ‘by night’. In Matthew, Joseph never says a word. He only listens and does what God says.
passages.ot:
The line is from Hosea 11:1: “When Israel was a child, I loved him, and out of Egypt I called My son.” In Hosea it looks back on the exodus, when God brought Israel, his ‘son’, out of Egypt. Hosea goes straight on to say that Israel kept turning away (Hosea 11:2).

So Matthew is not using Hosea as a prediction. He is using a pattern. Jesus lives out Israel's story again: down to Egypt, out of Egypt, through the water, into the wilderness. Where Israel the son wandered away, Jesus the Son will be faithful. Readers have called this a reading of Scripture as one long story, in which earlier events take on their full meaning later.
passages.asks: Jesus' first years were spent as a refugee in a foreign land, because a ruler wanted him dead. Christians have often drawn comfort from that, and a call. How does it shape the way you see people today who have fled danger with their children?

passages.happening:
When Herod realises the Magi have tricked him, he is furious. He sends soldiers to Bethlehem and the area around it, and they kill all the boys two years old and younger. He chose that age from what the Magi had told him about the star.

Matthew does not describe the killing. He tells it in one sentence, and then he gives the mothers' grief its place, quoting the prophet Jeremiah: “A voice is heard in Ramah, weeping and great mourning, Rachel weeping for her children, and refusing to be comforted, because they are no more” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
This is one of the saddest passages in the Bible, and Matthew lets it be sad. He does not explain it away or rush on.

Hearers who knew Herod would not be surprised he could do this. Josephus describes how, as Herod lay dying, he ordered the leading men of the nation locked in the arena at Jericho and killed at his death, so that the land would weep when he died. His sister released them instead (Jewish War 1.659-666).

No other ancient writer mentions the killing at Bethlehem. Bethlehem was a small village. Scholars estimate that the boys under two may have numbered a dozen or a few dozen. Many think such a crime, terrible for those families, would not have stood out among the larger killings Josephus records. Others doubt that it happened, because Josephus is silent and because it closely mirrors the story of Pharaoh killing the Hebrew boys (Exodus 1:22). The site tells the account as Matthew tells it, and says plainly what can and cannot be checked outside the Bible.

Rachel was the wife of Jacob, one of the mothers of Israel. She died giving birth and was buried “on the way to Ephrath (that is, Bethlehem)” (Genesis 35:19). Ramah was a town north of Jerusalem where, in Jeremiah's day, the captives were gathered to be marched off to Babylon (Jeremiah 40:1). So in Jeremiah, Rachel weeps for her children being carried into exile. Matthew hears her weeping again near her grave at Bethlehem.
passages.ot: The quotation is Jeremiah 31:15. But hearers who knew Jeremiah would also know the next lines. God says to Rachel: “Keep your voice from weeping and your eyes from tears” (Jeremiah 31:16), “So there is hope for your future” (Jeremiah 31:17). The same chapter promises a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31). Matthew quotes only the weeping. But the whole passage he points to moves from grief to hope. The child who escaped will one day give his own life, and promise that death will not have the last word.
passages.hard: Why would God protect Jesus and not the other children? Matthew does not answer that question, and it is honest to say so. He does three things instead. He does not blame God; he names Herod's rage as the cause. He does not hurry past the mothers; he gives their grief a whole verse of Scripture. And he places the story inside a larger one, in which this same child will suffer at the hands of rulers and die a cruel death, so that God is not watching suffering from far away. Christians have long remembered these children as the Holy Innocents. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like Rachel's, you are allowed to refuse comfort for a time, as she did. Please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service.
passages.asks: Rachel ‘refused to be comforted’, and Scripture does not scold her. Where do you need permission to grieve without rushing to an answer? And where in our world are children still dying because powerful people feel threatened? What would it mean to weep with those mothers, and to act?

passages.happening:
When Herod dies, the angel comes to Joseph in Egypt once more. Go back to the land of Israel, he says, “for those seeking the Child’s life are now dead” (verse 20). Joseph takes the family home.

But he hears that Archelaus, Herod's son, is now ruling Judea, and he is afraid to go there. Warned in another dream, he goes north to Galilee instead and settles in a town called Nazareth. Matthew says this fulfilled what the prophets said: “He will be called a Nazarene” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Joseph was right to be afraid of Archelaus. When Herod died, Rome split his kingdom among three sons. Archelaus got Judea. Josephus says that in his first months, at Passover, his soldiers killed about three thousand people in the temple courts (Antiquities 17.213-218). He ruled so badly that in AD 6 the emperor Augustus removed him and sent him into exile in Gaul. Galilee went to another son, Herod Antipas, who will appear later in Matthew (14:1-12).

Nazareth was a small, ordinary village in the hills of Galilee, not mentioned anywhere in the Old Testament. Another Gospel records a man asking whether anything good could come from there (John 1:46). So ‘Nazarene’ was not a grand title. It marked Jesus as a man from nowhere special.
passages.ot: The angel's words echo God's words to Moses: “Go back to Egypt, for all the men who sought to kill you are dead” (Exodus 4:19). Moses had fled a king who wanted him dead, and came back to rescue his people. Matthew wants you to hear Jesus' story with Moses' story underneath it.
passages.hard: ‘He will be called a Nazarene’ is not found word for word in any Old Testament book. Matthew seems to know this; he says ‘the prophets’, not one prophet. Readers have suggested several answers. Many think Matthew is playing on the Hebrew word netzer, ‘branch’, from Isaiah 11:1, where a Branch grows from the family of Jesse, David's father. The sound of netzer is close to Nazareth. Others link it to the Nazirites, people set apart to God (Numbers 6), though the words come from different roots. Others think Matthew means that, like the servant of the prophets, the Messiah would be looked down on, as Nazareth was. None of these is certain. All agree that Matthew sees God's hand even in where Jesus grew up.
passages.asks: God led the family by fear, by dreams, and by ordinary decisions about where it was safe to live. Jesus grew up in a town people sneered at. Where in your life has God worked through something that looked small or second best? And can you trust him with the places you would not have chosen?
